text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, PAH may cause no noticeable symptoms. As it progresses, symptoms often mimic other heart or lung conditions (such as asthma or deconditioning), including:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), initially during exercise or physical exertion and eventually while at rest
Fatigue and weakness or a feeling of heavy limbs
Chest pain, pressure, or tightness caused by an overworked, strained heart
Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly during physical activity
Heart palpitations or a fast, pounding pulse

text_blocks.snippet: As pressure builds and the right side of the heart faces increasing difficulty pumping blood, more severe signs can develop:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema) in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen due to fluid retention
Bluish or gray lips and skin (cyanosis) from low oxygen levels in the blood
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness (from an enlarged pulmonary artery pressing on chest nerves) in advanced cases

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about how specialists evaluate these signs through the American Lung Association PAH Guide or review broad clinical overviews via the Mayo Clinic Pulmonary Hypertension Overview.
